stories.headline: Christian Izien stars in strong defensive week for NFL stars with Africa ties
stories.summary: Detroit Lions safety Christian Izien - who is from Far Rockaway, Queens, but has always proudly represented Nigeria too - was a standout among many NFL stars with ties to Africa who shone in Week 3.
stories.body:
Detroit Lions safety Christian Izien - who is from Far Rockaway, Queens, but has always proudly represented Nigeria too - was a standout among many NFL stars with ties to Africa who shone in Week 3.

There were some highlights on offense too - notably from Jaxon Smith-Njigba and John Metchie III - but generally, this was a week where defense shone brightest for the continent's stars.

Africa Player of the Week: Christian Izien (Detroit Lions)

Izien was immensely influential for the Detroit Lions in their 31-24 win over the New York Jets, making a total of 11 tackles - nine of which were solo tackles - and defending one pass.

Izien - who has family ties to Nigeria - made three tackles for loss in addition to a vital intervention to prevent a touchdown right on the stroke of half-time. Geno Smith went for a Hail Mary with the Jets 10-7 down, but amid a sea of bodies from both teams, it was Izien who got to the ball first to tip it away.

His performance played a key role in the game ending in favour of the Lions - who are 2-1 for the season, with the Jets 1-2.

Africa Moment of the Week: Thomas Incoom and Maema Njongmeta (Carolina Panthers)

There were plenty of big hits to choose from among Africa's NFL stars. However, Incoom (born in Ghana) and Njongmeta (born in Cameroon) get the nod for collaborating in a moment which demonstrated what Africa has to offer the NFL.

As their Carolina Panthers faced the Cleveland Browns, Njongmeta forced a fumble with a huge hit on Malachi Corley and then Incoom - who had earlier set the tone with a massive hit himself - was on hand for the fumble recovery.

Although the Browns ultimately emerged victorious 21-18, it was not for any want of trying from the West African duo.

Honorable mentions

Jaxon Smith-Njigba - who proudly represents Sierra Leone, with which he has ties through his grandparents - scored two touchdowns among a total of 10 receptions for 128 yards. His Seattle Seahawks lost 33-31 to the Washington Commanders despite his contribution on offense and Uchenna Nwosu (ties to Nigeria) defending a pass.

John Metchie III - who is of Nigerian and Taiwanese descent and lived in Ghana as a young child - scored a touchdown for the Panthers in their defeat to the Browns. Nigerian-American outside linebacker Princely Umanmielen also made a notable contribution even in defeat for the Panthers, picking up a sack.

Adetomiwa Adebawore deserves special mention for his 1.5 sacks for the Indianapolis Colts in their 19-17 win over the Houston Texans.

Ruke Orhorhoro (Jacksonville Jaguars), Ogbo Okoronkwo (San Francisco 49ers), Eyioma Uwazurike (Denver Broncos), and Dayo Odeyingbo (Chicago Bears) - all of Nigerian descent - all picked up sacks in Week 3 wins.

Osa Odighizuwa, who contributed to the Niners' 36-30 win over the Arizona Cardinals with a pass defended, also has ties to Nigeria.

So, too, do players who had impressive moments on both sides of the Buffalo Bills' 24-16 win over the LA Chargers - Davison Igbinosun defended a pass for the winning side and Justin Eboigbe forced a fumble for the Chargers.

Africa-born player watch

Ghana's Incoom and Cameroon's Njongmeta did the continent proud with their performances for the Panthers in the Browns loss. It is worth noting that Ruke Orhorhoro, who picked up a sack for the Jacksonville Jaguars in their 35-6 thrashing of the New England Patriots, was born in Lagos - one of many players who flew the Nigerian flag high in Week 3.

stories.headline: Why is the Bahrain Grand Prix taking place in Malaysia, 4,000 miles away? F1's unusual race explained
stories.summary: Formula 1's next race has an odd quirk -- it is unofficially the rescheduled Bahrain Grand Prix, but it is taking place at Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit in Kuala Lumpur.
stories.body:
Formula 1's next race has an odd quirk. Look at the calendar and you'll see the rescheduled Bahrain Grand Prix. The only catch? It is taking place at Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit in Kuala Lumpur.

You don't have to be a geography buff to know those two places are not the same, nor are they close on the map. The bizarre event all comes down to global politics and is part of a wider situation that has left the destination of F1's season-ending races -- events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi -- uncertain, too.

Here's everything you need to know about F1's first "Middle Eastern" race of the year, and the current status of the final two races in the region which are meant to close the 2026 season.

- Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions

- Russell's win won't kick-start title challenge, but Baku rewards his faith in trying 2026

First things first, what are we calling this race?
Amusingly, perhaps slightly farcically, F1's next race will be called the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, held on Oct. 4, sandwiched between events in Baku and Singapore. It means another triple header on the calendar, with the season already due (as it stands) to feature Austin-Mexico City-Brazil, a gap, then Las Vegas-Qatar-Abu Dhabi.

While a slightly ridiculous naming convention, the event does mark a welcome and surprise return for the hugely popular Sepang circuit, which last hosted a race in 2017 after 18 years on the calendar. F1 understands the official flag next to the event will be Bahrain's, and the winner of the race will be considered to be a winner of the Bahrain Grand Prix in F1's official record books.

What national anthem will play before the event?
Exact plans remain to be seen, though sources have told ESPN that pre-race grid plans feature both the Bahrain and Malaysian flags, while Bahrain's national band is also in Malaysia for the event.

What happened to Bahrain's original race?
The decision not to hold races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia in April was a by-product of ongoing hostilities in the Middle East, triggered by a wave of attacks launched on Iran by the United States and Israel in March. That saw a number of countries in the region struck by Iran in response -- including Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. Bahrain's capital Manama was hit just weeks after it had hosted preseason testing.
As a result, F1 cancelled what would have been back-to-back races, the Bahrain Grand Prix on April 12 and Jeddah's Saudi Arabian Grand Prix on April 19. That left a four-week gap in the calendar between the Japanese Grand Prix and the Miami Grand Prix without a race. Importantly, at the time F1 made it clear the door was open for both events to happen later in the year should the situation in the region cool down.

Was rescheduling either event a realistic option?
Originally, F1 hoped it might be able to reschedule one or both events if and when the situation in the region cooled. Bahrain naturally was the easier option -- it's a permanent facility and, having hosted preseason and in anticipation of the event that should have taken place in April, some freight remains there which never left the nation state. That meant there was automatically a lot more flexibility around rearranging Bahrain if the opportunity had presented itself. As for Saudi Arabia, that was more complicated -- the Jeddah event is a street circuit around the city, for one thing, and street circuits naturally require a bit more lead-time in terms of preparation.

Sources have told ESPN that while Bahrain were happy to host an event wherever possible, Saudi's organisers had been set on rescheduling their race as a season-ending race. Even without a massive de-escalation in the Middle East, that presented big issues -- the season is already due to finish on Dec. 6 in Abu Dhabi. To avoid an unprecedented four straight races, a Saudi race would likely have needed to be held in the middle of December or nearer Christmas time, which has never happened before. Then there's Abu Dhabi's place as the season-ender -- the UAE venue has been the long-time finale event and pays a premium for the privilege. Sources have told ESPN Abu Dhabi was not thrilled at the idea of letting a regional rival take that from them. All of that is irrelevant now, anyway -- Abu Dhabi and Qatar's races both look set to be cancelled due to the same conflict (more on that below).

Why did Malaysia help Bahrain out?
It might seem like a strange link-up on the surface, but the two nations actually share a close diplomatic relationship stretching back to 1974. Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa and Malaysia King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar reportedly have a strong personal rapport. Sources have told ESPN the plan was first discussed in a conversation between the pair and a plan quickly unfolded from there. Bahrain had a race to reschedule and Malaysia had a beloved circuit completely free to step in. Malaysia offered to split the cost with Bahrain and it was seen as a win-win -- a good way to mark strong diplomatic ties between the two nations, while Bahrain gets to say it retained its grand prix on the 2026 calendar and Sepang gets the feel-good rub of stepping in and helping Bahrain and Formula 1 out in an hour of need.

Why was Bahrain so keen to hold a race, even if not on its own circuit?
Bahrain has been invested in F1 for a long time now. It first hosted a race in 2004 and has become a mainstay on the calendar, often as the season-opener, as well as becoming a regular and reliable preseason test venue. The nation state is also deeply intertwined with the sport -- Bahrain's sovereign wealth fund, Mumtalakat Holding Company, is majority owner of the McLaren team and full owner of the wider McLaren Group.

The scale of its involvement in F1 is far deeper than is currently the case in Saudi. But it wasn't just Bahrain that felt a need to get something sorted. The rearrangement is big from a contractual perspective for Formula 1 as well. The sport's commercial agreement with its 11 teams and its global broadcasters says the season cannot drop below 22 races -- should that ever happen, the financial cost for the sport would be severe. Bahrain and Saudi had already both been cancelled -- with Qatar and Abu Dhabi both likely to be canned at the end of the season, the sport effectively needed to find two replacements in quick time. Malaysia and Bahrain doing a deal meant F1 only had to find one race to finish the season with, should those other two events be cancelled as expected. As we will come to, easier options in Europe existed to fill a one-race gap.

What was Sepang like, and why did it stop hosting F1 in the first place?
Sepang enjoyed 18 years as a Formula 1 host between 1999 and 2017 and quickly established itself as a popular venue, with drivers loving its fast, flowing corners, while it boasts numerous places to overtake. Sepang actually was unlucky in the timing of its departure from the calendar -- Formula 1 was in a much less lucrative place at the time.

Liberty Media had only just taken over with a grand plan for the sport's growth, which has come to pass in the years since Covid. In 2017 things were not quite so rosy as they are now -- then-CEO of Sepang, Razlan Razali, told Reuters at the time: "It's hard to sell this kind of event and to get bums on the seats. It's not worth the investment at the moment." Of course, F1 has enjoyed stratospheric growth since the pandemic and most races are easy sellouts, with huge revenues and 11 teams all worth north of $1 billion (£753 million). Hindsight is 20-20, as they say.

Does this one-off return make Malaysia a candidate to host events again in the future?
It's hard to say for now. This event certainly can't hurt, and it's clear the event is in F1's good graces at the moment for stepping in. But it's not simply a case of it being fast-tracked to the front of the line for a future event. F1's calendar is already jam-packed at 24 events -- next year Portugal and Türkiye return, and F1 boss Stefano Domenicali often says there is a queue of potential venues waiting for a spot to open up, with the sport keen to prioritise an event in Africa in future if a viable venue materialises. Then there's Singapore, which may not be thrilled at the prospect of hosting a race so close to a neighbour every year. When Sepang was a regular host, Singapore and Malaysia were often next to each other on the calendar, but rarely just a week apart.
Isn't F1's season finishing in the Middle East as it stands? What about those two races?
As it stands, yes, although it seems likely that will change in the coming weeks after F1 bosses were told that they can expect a final decision by mid-October. The calendar as it stands says Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6 will close the season, but F1 has been delaying a decision on both events as it monitors the situation in the region and there was hope the events could both go ahead as planned.

The World Endurance Championship, the series which holds the famous Le Mans 24 Hours, has already cancelled a race in Qatar that was due to be held in November. Sources have told ESPN that Italian circuit Imola will hold the season-ending race should Qatar and Abu Dhabi be cancelled. In that scenario, the race would take place on Dec. 6, the existing spot for Abu Dhabi's race. While eyebrows in the paddock have been raised at hosting a race in northern Italy in December, logistically the race presents an easy option, with all 11 teams based in Europe.

- Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur vents frustration over Christian Horner's F1 job search

- Charles Leclerc admits Ferrari's rivals have taken 'big steps forwards': 'We must not lie to ourselves'

Is Imola really the only option to step in?
Many in F1 have wondered the same thing, but the circuit has only just dropped off the calendar as a grand prix host, so its infrastructure is in place. Weather is far from ideal, with sunlight at a minimum and snow a regular feature, but the circuit has close ties to the sport which probably helped shuffle the historic venue to the front of the line -- it is the hometown of F1 CEO Domenicali and Ferrari's unofficial home race, given its close proximity to Ferrari's Maranello headquarters. Still, others wondered if other venues might be more appropriate.

F1 is due to race in Las Vegas the weekend before Thanksgiving, leaving many to speculate whether F1 could stay in America and race at Austin's Circuit of the Americas (COTA), which is already hosting a race on Oct. 24. However, COTA does not appear to have put itself forward nor does it appear to have been asked by F1 to stand in. Portugal's Portimao circuit was also floated as an option, but stepping in to host an event in December would have threatened the timeline of the renovations and upgrades the venue is doing in order to host a race next season. Imola, which dropped off the calendar after its 2025 race, has therefore emerged as the likely season-ender.

stories.headline: Schlittler and Rice torment hometown team as Yankees beat rival Red Sox 9-0 in playoff opener
stories.summary: — Cam Schlittler pitched another playoff gem against the Boston Red Sox, and Ben Rice also burned their hometown team with a late grand slam and six RBI as the New York Yankees opened this Wild Card Series rematch with a 9-0 victory Tuesday night.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- — Cam Schlittler pitched another playoff gem against the Boston Red Sox, and Ben Rice also burned their hometown team with a late grand slam and six RBI as the New York Yankees opened this Wild Card Series rematch with a 9-0 victory Tuesday night.


With the Yankees minus star slugger Aaron Judge because of a calf injury, Rice homered twice, doubled and finished with four hits to power the offense. No. 9 batter Austin Wells drove in two runs for New York, and 21-year-old rookie George Lombard Jr. had three hits in his postseason debut.


Rice and Schlittler were both raised among Red Sox fans in Massachusetts and went to college in New England before getting plucked by the Yankees out of Boston's backyard in baseball's amateur draft.


Schlittler, a clear frontrunner for the AL Cy Young Award after leading the league with a 1.95 ERA, struck out 10 and walked one in 6 1/3 innings. He allowed only two hits while throwing 117 pitches — 10 more than his previous career high and most by a Yankees postseason starter since Hall of Fame lefty CC Sabathia threw 121 in the 2012 AL Division Series against Baltimore.


The major league high this season was 120 by Dylan Cease for Toronto at Boston in July.

stories.headline: Transfer rumors, news: Real Madrid eye Van Dijk on free transfer at end of season
stories.summary: Real Madrid are hoping they can sign Virgil van Dijk when his Liverpool contract expires at the end of the season. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
Real Madrid are hoping they can sign Virgil van Dijk when his Liverpool contract expires at the end of the season. Plus, Gilberto Mora is subject to interest from Liverpool.

Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Liverpool skipper Virgil van Dijk could join Real Madrid on a free transfer when his contract expires at the end of the 2026-27 season, according to Mundo Deportivo. The 35-year-old central defender has not received an offer of a renewal from Liverpool officials, suggesting that his time at the club could be coming to a natural conclusion. Madrid boss Jose Mourinho, who already has Van Dijk's former teammates Trent Alexander-Arnold and Ibrahima Konaté in his defensive ranks, both also signed at the end of their Liverpool contracts, is interested in adding another center back. However, Madrid are not the only club monitoring the situation, with AC Milan, Galatasaray and Inter Miami also mentioned as potential destinations. Van Dijk joined Liverpool in 2018 and helped transform the club's fortunes, playing his part in the club winning every domestic trophy as well as the UEFA Champions League, UEFA Super Cup and FIFA World Club Cup.

- Liverpool are interested in Club Tijuana and Mexico international midfielder Gilberto Mora, according to Football Insider. The Reds are said to be admirers of the 17-year-old, but there is significant competition emerging in the race for his signature, with Real Madrid, Barcelona, and Paris Saint-Germain also keen. The Liga MX side are expected to part ways with him at the end of the season when they believe his value will be at its highest. Mora impressed at the World Cup in the summer and has made an impressive start to the new campaign with five goals in seven matches.

- Real Madrid are monitoring the situation of Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, TEAMtalk reports. Madrid are assessing the transfer market for a long-term option between the posts, and they see the 27-year-old as a strong candidate to succeed Thibaut Courtois due to his experience in the Champions League. Whether City part ways with Donnarumma could hinge on their punishment after they were found guilty on Tuesday of almost all 115 financial charges brought against them by the Premier League. City have until Friday to appeal.

- Barcelona defender Jules Koundé has been placed on the shortlist of Bayern Munich, Diario Sport reports. The Bundesliga club have kept close tabs on the 27-year-old for some time, and they are lining up an approach for him as a potential future successor to defender Kim Min-jae. Kounde signed a new five-year contract back in August 2025, but having failed to establish himself as a starter in La Liga this season, a switch to the Allianz Arena could become a possibility in the January transfer window.

- Manchester United are weighing up a move for Crystal Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta, according to TEAMtalk. Mateta, 29, is seen as a potential option to provide competition for Benjamin Sesko as well as provide attacking depth to manager Michael Carrick's squad. Clubs in Saudi Arabia are also monitoring the situation, with Mateta keen to search for a new challenge away from Selhurst Park, where he has nine months remaining on his current contract.

- Juventus are preparing to make midfielder Teun Koopmeiners available for transfer in January, Gazzetta dello Sport reports. The Serie A club are reportedly disappointed with the 28-year-old's form and will look to sanction an exit if his performances don't "significantly" improve. Everton, Newcastle, and Monaco checked on his situation in the summer, and the Bianconeri could be willing to accept a loan offer due to his €5.7 million-per-season salary.

stories.headline: Reeve laments Lynx 'don't quite have right group' after latest playoff flop
stories.summary: The Lynx became the first No. 1 seed in league history to be swept in its opening series, marking another heartbreaking playoff exit for the third straight year.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- As the clock dwindled to zero in Tuesday night's first-round matchup against the New York Liberty, Minnesota Lynx standouts Napheesa Collier, Kayla McBride and Courtney Williams found each other on the Barclays Center court and shared a collective embrace, cementing yet another heartbreaking Lynx playoff exit for the third straight year.

Minnesota became the first No. 1 seed in WNBA playoff history to be swept in its opening series, losing 87-71 in a must-win Game 2 to New York. With the Liberty also comfortably winning Game 1, the games marked the first time in franchise history that the Lynx lost consecutive playoff contests by 15 or more points.

"We became a great regular-season team this year," coach Cheryl Reeve said, "and we ran into the wrong team."

Minnesota looked the part of title contenders for much of the season, improving to 31-7 in late August behind the stellar play of Olivia Miles, the unanimous Rookie of the Year, and Reeve's latest coaching masterclass, which earned her Coach of the Year honors for the fifth time.

But after a rocky past few weeks in which they almost fell to the No. 2 seed, the Lynx were for the second straight year unable to reach the WNBA Finals despite being the best team in the league during the regular season.

"I thought the playoffs would be hard for our team, regardless of who we were playing in the first round," Reeve said. "We probably needed a little better matchup to do some of the things that we did all season long, but that's not how it works."

Earlier this season, Reeve became the winningest coach in WNBA history and was inducted into the Women's Basketball Hall of Fame. She has led the Lynx franchise to four championships -- in 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2017 -- and nearly a fifth in 2024, when the team came one controversial foul call away from beating the Liberty in a championship-deciding Game 5 in Brooklyn.

But Reeve acknowledged Tuesday that while championships are in Minnesota's DNA, she hasn't viewed the past few years with a championship-or-bust mentality, particularly given those teams have arguably overachieved.

"There are sometimes when you have that team and that would be the case, you should feel that way," Reeve said. "I have not felt like we've had that team over these three years, and so what we're doing is sort of maybe exceeding expectations in the regular season, and then when it comes playoffs, maybe we don't quite have the right group to be effective.

"I just know we have some work to do. I have to help us. I have to get us the appropriate help to do it, make the hard decisions to do that. I couldn't get us there in this series, and so it's on me. I have to help them win in the playoffs ... both as an executive [president of basketball operations] and as the coach, and I'll find a way to do that."

Asked why it has been difficult to translate regular-season success to winning championships, Collier -- the Lynx's perennial MVP candidate who returned midseason after offseason ankle surgeries -- said she wasn't sure what to attribute that to.

"I don't know. I feel like if we knew the answer to that, we would be translating it over," Collier said. "That's something that obviously we have to figure out."

Granted, the Lynx's matchup against New York was an unfavorable one: The Liberty are known for their length at nearly every position, even bringing 6-foot-11 Han Xu off the bench, and their prowess at defending the rim. Reeve pointed to New York's ability to "render ineffective" both Miles, who typically thrives around the basket, and All-Star forward Natasha Howard as Minnesota's undoing.

"I think their size really bothered us," Miles said. "We didn't really know what coverage worked best. We were switching, we were hedging, we were playing drop, trying to throw a lot of things at them. Their size really is imposing."

New York also wasn't a traditional No. 8 seed -- seven games separated Minnesota and New York in the standings and only two separated the No. 5 and No. 8 seeds. The Liberty's big three of Breanna Stewart, Jonquel Jones and Sabrina Ionescu scored or assisted on 70 points for New York, whereas the Lynx had 71 as a team.

Meanwhile, Collier didn't look like her assertive, dominant self this series. On Tuesday, she got into foul trouble in the third quarter, making a late rally more difficult. And Miles, who so often played beyond her years this summer, looked like a rookie playing in her first postseason games.

"Their big three were really, really good," Reeve said, "and we kind of struggled to have a big three. That's just not a great place to be."

Said Miles: "You could tell for a lot of us that we're playing tight and stressed and afraid of losing instead of trying to win. Maybe from my end, that's a lack of experience. But I think we wanted to win so bad that we almost cared too much, honestly, and cared in the wrong ways, and it really limited us."

Miles finished the series with totals of 16 points, two assists, five turnovers and seven fouls. It was what Reeve said can be a learning experience for her but one that doesn't erase her body of work this season.

"Everyone wants to win all the time. That's just not how it works," Miles said. "Sometimes I have to have experiences like this that hurt this bad to get me to where I want to be."

Minnesota faces a fascinating offseason ahead with Williams, McBride and Howard all under contract through 2027, plus Miles still on her rookie deal. Collier, meanwhile, will hit free agency and cannot be cored by the team. She has been noncommittal when asked about her desire to stay with Minnesota beyond this year.

Time will tell whether that moment with Collier, McBride and Williams embracing on the Barclays Court, with a WNBA championship out of reach once more, will be the lasting image of the Lynx as we know it.

"We got to each other at special times in our career," McBride said of the trio. "What we've created in Minnesota, our culture, when people come into it, they love it. They love being a part of what we've been able to grow these last couple years, and that's not lost on me."

stories.headline: Former draftee slams AFL over concussion plight
stories.summary: An AFL draftee whose life was upended by a concussion injury says he "was so close to ending everything".
stories.body:
An AFL draftee whose life was upended by a concussion injury says he "was so close to ending everything".

Aiden O'Driscoll, who had to retire because of a devastating training injury without making his AFL debut, also slammed the league as an "absolute joke".

"The last couple of years I've experienced nothing but pain, and I've explained it multiple times to you. You're supposed to help AFL players through hardship, not leave them with absolutely nothing," O'Driscoll wrote in his extensive Instagram post.

His comments came a day after Geelong announced defender Jake Kolodjashnij had retired.

Last month, the Cats were fined $140,000 and current AFL chairman Craig Drummond apologised after it emerged the club had agreed to a secret concussion waiver with Kolodjashnij. Drummond was Geelong president at the time the agreement was struck.

The Geelong controversy highlighted the complexity and sensitivity around contact sport's concussion crisis.

The Western Bulldogs recruited O'Driscoll in the 2023 draft. But a head injury that summer left him with significant ongoing health problems and the club announced in May, 2024 that he had retired on medical grounds.

"The doctors described my concussion as 'one of the worst' they've seen, with eight micro brain bleeds, and (a) fracture behind my ear," O'Driscoll wrote.

"From a medical point of view, losing my career, my identity plus going through the symptoms I have, you'd think the AFL would be useful with some support?

O'Driscoll added it took the AFL six weeks to find him a psychologist.

"Through this period, I was grieving the most, it got to the point where I started questioning my life? If it was worth living?," he wrote.

"I was so close to ending everything, I would've been free from all the pain/trauma. My family/close friends and partners honestly kept me here."

Melbourne premiership player Angus Brayshaw also had to retire in 2024 because of his concussion issues.

In his emotional toast to other retiring players at the Brownlow Medal function that year, Brayshaw referred to O'Driscoll by name.

"I know a few other past players that are dealing with the same issues as I am," O'Driscoll said.

"AFL it's time to step up! I'm a 21-year-old that can't keep suffering each week. While you're at it, help the other past players that need support."

O'Driscoll added he had been told at 18 never to play contact sport again.

The AFL and the players' association were contacted for comment.

stories.headline: Kessler talks up Lakers' title hopes behind 'nasty' defense
stories.summary: New addition Walker Kessler is convinced the Lakers have the right guys to be "a nasty defensive team" and a contender in the Western Conference this season.
stories.body:
EL SEGUNDO, Calif. -- The Los Angeles Lakers' offense has thrived since Luka Doncic arrived in 2025, but center Walker Kessler needed only one day of training camp to be convinced the team's defense will hold up its end of the bargain this season.

"Listen, I think we're going to be a nasty defensive team," Kessler said Tuesday. "I think people aren't taking into account how good our perimeter defense is going to be. A lot of guys are very smart on the perimeter and positionally can play really good defense. We have guys who are just ball hawks."

During JJ Redick's two seasons as coach, the Lakers have ranked above average in offensive efficiency and below average in defensive efficiency. After a transformative summer that saw the departure of LeBron James and several other veteran players, the Lakers are hoping to establish a more aggressive defensive identity with a rebuilt roster that includes Doncic, guard Austin Reaves, Kessler and a deep group of young wings.

Redick said Tuesday that his first goal during training camp was to "establish our defensive principles." With both forward spots in the starting lineup open for competition, Redick said he met with the team's wings last week to give them their marching orders.

"They understood the assignment today," he said. "That was exciting. They set the tone for us defensively. There was a lot of physicality, a lot of grabbing and holding, and a lot of disruption without gambling."

The 7-foot-2 Kessler, who was traded by the Utah Jazz to the Lakers this summer, will serve as the back-line rim protector after averaging 2.4 blocks per game during his first four seasons.

"The paint is kind of closed when [Kessler] is on the court," Doncic said.

From there, Doncic's remade supporting cast includes defensive specialists Jarred Vanderbilt and Matisse Thybulle as well as free agent additions Quentin Grimes, Sandro Mamukelashvili, Collin Sexton and Ziaire Williams. Kevon Looney, a veteran center who won two championships with the Golden State Warriors, will back up Kessler.

Kessler praised Looney for his "mind and positioning," Vanderbilt for his skill defending all five positions, and Thybulle, Grimes, Sexton and Williams for their ability to apply defensive pressure.

"Having those guys that can steal the ball ... [and] when they do get beat, be able to recover, it makes my job a lot easier," he said. "It's a lot easier to block a shot when a dude has someone on his hip instead of an open lane towards the basket."

The Lakers boasted the NBA's No. 3 defense when they won the 2020 championship and the No. 1 defense during the 2020-21 regular season. But their performance on that end has slipped noticeably in the years that followed.

Los Angeles fired Frank Vogel as coach after ranking 21st in defense during the 2021-22 season, then fired his successor, Darvin Ham, after ranking 17th in defense in 2023-24. The Lakers finished 20th on defense last season, their first full campaign after trading All-Star big man Anthony Davis to the Dallas Mavericks for Doncic.

Kessler was confident the Lakers "definitely can be a contender" in a Western Conference that includes title favorites with elite defenses such as the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs.

"I think we have a lot of great tools and versatility," he said. "The guys are already getting along. Connection makes championship teams."

stories.headline: NRL Midweek Mail Grand Final: Halves injuries put Brooks on Penrith's radar
stories.summary: Daniel Tupou insists the result of the Grand Final will not decide whether he plays on, while Robert Toia is modest about his extraordinary talents.
stories.body:
The NRL rarely stands still.

Between training sessions, media appearances, and behind-the-scenes conversations, new storylines often begin to emerge before the weekend arrives.

Throughout the week, ESPN will be gathering notes, insights, and updates from around the competition heading into the NRL's Grand Final weekend.

Panthers emerge in Brooks race

Penrith have emerged as a potential destination for Luke Brooks should the veteran half depart Manly ahead of the 2027 season.

ESPN understands the Panthers are interested in Brooks, per multiple sources, as uncertainty continues around the playmaker's future at the Sea Eagles.

Brooks remains contracted to Manly through 2027, meaning any move for next season would require an early release, with Jamal Fogarty and highly rated youngster Joey Walsh the focus of the Sea Eagles' halves plans.

The Penrith link comes amid uncertainty surrounding their halves stocks for 2027.

Nathan Cleary and Blaize Talagi face lengthy injury recoveries, while Jack Cole will depart for the Perth Bears at season's end, leaving Jack Cogger as the Panthers' other established halves option.

Raiders eye Storm young gun

Canberra are keeping tabs on Melbourne Storm prop Josiah Pahulu ahead of the November 1 transfer window.

ESPN understands the Raiders are interested in the highly rated 22-year-old, who remains contracted to Melbourne through the end of 2027.

Pahulu joined the Storm from the Gold Coast midway through 2025 and has since continued his development in Melbourne's system.

Eligible to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 from November 1, Pahulu has emerged as a player of interest for Canberra as clubs begin positioning themselves ahead of the market opening.

Amone commits to the Dragons

St George Illawarra have retained promising youngster Viliami Amone on a one-year deal for 2027 despite interest from several rival clubs, ESPN understands.

The younger brother of former Dragons playmaker Junior Amone was part of the club's Jersey Flegg side that claimed the 2026 minor premiership.

He played in the second row during the season and also earned four NSW Cup appearances as he progressed through the Dragons' pathways.

Tupou says Grand Final result won't decide his future

Daniel Tupou has put talks over his playing future on hold until after Sunday's Grand Final, but says the result will have no bearing on whether he continues next season.

Asked if winning a premiership might change his decision, the 35-year-old said:

"Not at all. I've just parked it for now in this finals series. Once this game's done, then I'll get back onto it."

Tupou said he still believes he has another year in him and confirmed family and friends have encouraged him to keep playing. For now, his focus is on a fourth Grand Final appearance with the Roosters.

Toia rejects top-three centre talk ahead of grand final

Robert Toia has played his way into conversations about the NRL's best centres, but the Roosters youngster believes a top-three ranking is premature.

"It's pretty good to hear, to be honest," Toia said of the praise.

"But I think that's exaggerated. I wouldn't say I'm a top-three centre.

"I feel like I've been playing somewhat good footy, but there's still a lot to show and still more to come."

Sunday's Grand Final offers a test against Bradman Best, whom Toia named among the most difficult centres to defend because of his size, speed and agility.

The pair have never met off the field, but Toia said he loves the matchup and is looking forward to measuring himself against the Newcastle star.

Familiar faces on the other side

Tupou said the Roosters are pleased to see former teammate Sandon Smith thriving at Newcastle, praising him as a player who delivered in big games during his time at the club. That goodwill will be set aside on Sunday.

Tupou is also preparing to face Dom Young, whose return to the Knights has set up a direct contest with his former Roosters teammate.

He said he did not know the details behind Young's exit and declined to speculate, but expects "a great battle" against the winger.

stories.headline: Cowboys' Schottenheimer 'aligned' with Jones after Rio gaffes
stories.summary: Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said he would "be better" after meeting with Jerry Jones about questionable late-game coaching decisions in Sunday's loss to the Ravens.
stories.body:
FRISCO, Texas -- Dallas Cowboys owner and general manager Jerry Jones did not mask disappointment with the decisions made in the final 28 seconds of Sunday's loss to the Baltimore Ravens in the NFL's first game in Rio de Janeiro.

Jones and coach Brian Schottenheimer went through the end-of-game decisions, from the playcalling after the Cowboys faced first-and-goal from the 2, to Dak Prescott's third-down throwaway that led to a tying field goal, to how the subsequent kickoff and seven seconds were handled, allowing the Ravens to kick a winning field goal with a second to play.

"There is no explanation you're satisfied with. None," Jones said on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas on Tuesday morning. "Let's be sure that we all understand that. [The coaches] don't have one that they're satisfied with. ... But there's an evaluation of how not to make the same mistakes again. You can't get that back. [There's] no way to get it back. What you can do is use it ... to get better. That's what's being done."

Schottenheimer accepted responsibility with Jones and publicly in his first comments after the team's return from Brazil.

"I'm man enough to take mistakes. I make a lot of mistakes. I'm certainly not perfect," Schottenheimer said. "And I know one thing, Jerry and I had a very good conversation about it. I explained it. He understands. He understands that there was a mistake that was made, and he was terrific. Great, sound advice. I value him. He's been around the game a long time, just like I have, and he's seen a lot of stuff.

"And so to me, that shows that he and I are aligned very closely. This will make me better. I'll be better. And again, I'm looking forward to lining up and playing this week against the Texans."

Schottenheimer added, "I hurt our chance to win that game and I'll be better. And I'm better than that. I'm better than I performed in the last 28 seconds."

After the game, Schottenheimer said he "overcoached" Prescott on the third-down pass to George Pickens that was a throwaway.

"I trust Dak Prescott completely, so it was the word that I chose, which I'm not going to give away," Schottenheimer said. "The words that we say have meaning, and when I said the word, it put him into a mindset that he doesn't play with. He doesn't play that way. He doesn't play the game that way. And so that's what I would change."

After Brandon Aubrey tied the score with a 23-yard field goal, the Cowboys had him kick the ball through the end zone for a touchback. The Ravens took over at their own 35, and quarterback Lamar Jackson hit receiver Zay Flowers for a 27-yard completion to set up the 56-yard kick from Tyler Loop with one second left.

In retrospect, Aubrey's kickoff should have been short to burn time off the clock.

Schottenheimer said his emotions of the third-down call affected the kickoff decision, adding that the communication between special teams coordinator Nick Sorensen and game management coordinator Ryan Feder was not good enough either.

"My dad had a rule -- one play at a time," he said, referring to former NFL coach Marty Schottenheimer. "He talked a lot about it, because it happened to him. He made a decision on a play, it didn't go good, he was pissed off about it and it affected another decision. I think that's kind of what happened to me. So I'll take accountability for it. It's football and life. It's what happens."

As he did after the game, Schottenheimer did not express regret over defensive coordinator Christian Parker's call that allowed the completion to Flowers.

"I think the coverage was OK," he said. "We played way too tight, and there was an error on that play where we should have made the ball go to the low underneath guy, not the deep one."

Schottenheimer has been a head coach for only 20 games, although he is in his 25th year in the NFL. Parker, 34, is a first-time coordinator. So far, the defense has not performed consistently, but Jones said he remained confident in what his team could accomplish this season.

Injuries have hit the defense with safety Jalen Thompson (hamstring) probably headed to injured reserve with a designation to return. Schottenheimer said defensive tackle Jonathan Bullard could sit out a couple of weeks because of a calf strain. The Cowboys could see safety Malik Hooker (forearm) and linebacker DeMarvion Overshown return this week against Houston, but the team worked out five players, including former Cowboys safety Juanyeh Thomas and Bengals linebacker Germaine Pratt.

The Cowboys' next three opponents -- the Texans, Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Green Bay Packers -- have one win combined this season. The New York Giants lost quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season to a knee injury, and Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels is out because of an elbow injury sustained against Dallas.

"We are very much in the hunt, and I say that principally based upon the way I feel about our team, as much or more than what's happening with the other teams," Jones told The Fan on Tuesday. "Philadelphia has things that they want to work on just as the Giants do, just as we do. It makes you see how health is a factor. Availability is a factor. And we're just getting started."

stories.headline: Esteban Ocon to leave Haas but vows F1 career isn't over
stories.summary: Esteban Ocon will leave Haas at the end of the season, the driver and team confirmed on Wednesday, with the Frenchman defiantly vowing "this is absolutely not the end of my Formula 1 career."
stories.body:
Esteban Ocon will leave Haas at the end of the season, the driver and team confirmed on Wednesday, with the Frenchman defiantly vowing "this is absolutely not the end of my Formula 1 career."

Ocon's departure will leave him without an F1 race seat for 2027 as there are no available options left.

Haas is expected to sign Formula 2 title contender Rafael Camara in Ocon's place, although no final decision has been made and an announcement is not expected to come this week. Like Ocon's teammate Oliver Bearman, Brazilian driver Camara, 21, is part of Haas engine partner Ferrari's junior academy.

Ocon, who had already declared himself a free agent ahead of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix last week, looks likely to seek an F1 reserve or test role in the hope of a 2028 seat opening up, although he is yet to confirm his short-term plans.

He suggested external factors have held him back from performing to his best at Haas, although he did not elaborate.

"I leave this project with my head held high and proud of my performances in what were not always the easiest of circumstances for various reasons and factors outside of my control," Ocon, 30, said in a statement on Wednesday.

"My immediate focus is the next race weekend. I will continue to work hard with the team, maximise every opportunity, and keep extracting every bit of performance from the car. There are still many races to go this season and, as always, I will give it my everything behind the wheel for myself and for my team.

"I am still motivated. I am still hungry. This is absolutely not the end of my Formula 1 career."

Ocon will talk to the media on Thursday ahead of F1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. His F1 career started with minnows Manor in 2016. The French driver had been tipped for big things as a youngster, entering F1 as a Mercedes junior, but his career never lived up to those lofty expectations, with a top drive never opening up for him.

He joined Haas at the start of 2025 after a long stint with Alpine which included his solitary F1 win at the 2021 Hungarian Grand Prix. However, he struggled to perform consistently alongside Bearman and the team was on the verge of signing Yuki Tsunoda in his place for 2026, only for Ayao Komatsu to change his mind and offer Ocon a chance to prove himself under F1's new regulation changes this year.

Ocon has not done enough this season to secure a third season. Komatsu paid tribute to Ocon's contribution and said his experience has helped the team adjust to F1's new rules.

"I'd like to thank Esteban for everything he's contributed to the team since joining us in 2025," Komatsu said. "His professionalism and commitment have proved valuable as we continue to grow as an organization. Together this year we tackled the challenge of a major regulation change, where Esteban's driving experience and inputs were significant as we've worked hard to develop the VF-26 across the season. There's still plenty of racing ahead, and our focus remains on working together to maximize every opportunity through to the final race of the year."

The Ocon news -- and Camara's expected signing in his place -- is one of the last bits of the 2027 grid to be confirmed.

Red Bull junior outfit Racing Bulls and Cadillac are yet to confirm their lineups for next season, but neither appears to be an option for Ocon in terms of a race seat. Racing Bulls is still to decide whether to continue with Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson, with Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov waiting in the wings. Cadillac is understood to be weighing up whether to extend Valtteri Bottas for a second season or to promote American test driver Colton Herta to a 2028 race seat.

- F1 2027 driver lineups: Who has a seat - and who's out of contract?

- Ferrari gives Fred Vasseur 'full confidence' amid Christian Horner speculation

Much of the driver market this year hinged on the decisions of world champions Max Verstappen and Fernando Alonso, but both drivers have signed deals to stay with Red Bull and Aston Martin respectively which has drastically limited movement elsewhere.

Alonso's future was one a lot of drivers in the midfield had been keeping an eye on. Although the Spanish driver delayed that decision, it seemed clear which way the wind was blowing shortly after F1's summer break when Williams drivers Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz committed to another season, and when Alpine -- the strongest candidate for Alonso's signature beyond Aston Martin -- signed Franco Colapinto to another year.

Alonso finally confirmed on Tuesday he will contest another Formula 1 season with Aston Martin in 2027. His future beyond that is unclear, meaning 45-year-old Alonso will likely hold the keys to the driver market again next season.

stories.headline: Five stats: Why USMNT should be excited about Cavan Sullivan
stories.summary: Is the hype around Cavan Sullivan's USMNT future too much? No, it's actually not enough -- and here are five reasons why.
stories.body:
There's something incredible happening in MLS right now, and the average World Cup watcher probably has no clue.

Seriously, think about all of the people you know who are "sports fans" but maybe not "soccer fans" -- the ones who root hard for the U.S. men's national team every four years and know the names of their four or five best players.

Sure, they probably still can't pronounce the last name of manager Mauricio Pochettino, but they watched tons of soccer this summer. The World Cup had so many games, and finally, it was all aligned with our time zones. These people now have opinions about VAR, England's prevent defense and the general moral fiber of the Argentina national team.

They're primed to care about soccer, especially American soccer, and especially a kind of greatness we've never seen before from a player of a certain age. No, I'm not talking about Lionel Messi, who somehow (1) might still be the greatest soccer player in the world, (2) is easily the greatest 39-year-old soccer player we've ever seen, and (3) continues to play soccer every week, across North America, without having any effect on North American sports discourse.

No, I'm talking about Cavan Sullivan, the 16-year-old phenom who, somehow, still feels as if he's being underhyped.

The history of American soccer is filled with players who were overpromised and couldn't do anything but underdeliver, but this is different. It's not just that we, Americans, have never seen someone like Sullivan. No, the wider soccer world -- the rest of the entire world -- rarely ever sees someone like Sullivan.

Here are some numbers for why you should get excited:

1,675 minutes
As I like to often say: The best predictor of future stardom is minutes players at a young age.

Take the three front-runners for this year's Ballon d'Or. Harry Kane was playing and scoring goals for Millwall in the Championship during his age-18 season. Lamine Yamal is 19 -- right now. And Kylian Mbappé broke out for Monaco during his age-17 season.

Sullivan is currently in his age-16 season (defined by your age at the start of the campaign). And so far, he has played 1,675 league minutes in MLS.

The site FBref has data for what they call the "Next 14" -- essentially, the most competitive leagues in the world after Europe's Big Five -- that goes back to the beginning of the current century, if not more. Only 21 outfield players have played more league minutes than Sullivan, who still has at least eight games left in his season. If we expand the dataset to include the Big Five, then only five other players -- Eduardo Camavinga, Alex Song, Gavi, Lamine Yamal, and Nuri Sahin -- have played more minutes than Sullivan before their age-17 season.

The leader, among all of these players? Freddy Adu had played 5,448 minutes by the end of his age-16 season.

€1.54 billion
Though we don't have much useful leaguewide data dating to 2006, when Adu was wrapping up his age-16 season, I do feel confident in saying the following: MLS is a lot better than it was 20 years ago.

Heck, it's a lot better than it was even 10 years ago. Per a recent analysis by Michael Caley: In 2016, the average combined transfer value of the median MLS team (as estimated by the site Transfermarkt) was significantly lower than the average team in the first divisions in Mexico, Belgium, Portugal and the Netherlands. Since then, the league has essentially caught up to Belgium and Mexico in transfer value, and it has surpassed Portugal and the Netherlands.

Though the biggest teams in those European leagues are still way better and richer than any MLS side -- thanks to Champions League prize money -- the average match that Cavan Sullivan plays in MLS is probably tougher than what he'd face were he playing for Benfica, Porto or PSV.

All in all, the combined estimated transfer values of all 30 MLS clubs is €1.54 billion -- or about €51.3 million per team.

12 goals and assists
For the Big Five leagues, FBref has goal-and-assist data dating to at least the mid-1990s for Ligue 1, for the entirety of the Premier League since its breakaway from the English Football League in 1992, and the late 1980s for Italy, Germany and Spain.

Over that stretch, the record for goals+assists before a player's age-17 season comes from Bojan Krkic, who scored 10 goals and created three more in his early years -- right at the beginning of Pep Guardiola's dominance with Barcelona. Next after him is a tie between Yamal and Wayne Rooney's Everton years, at 10.

Sullivan currently has 12 -- a nearly even split between seven goals and five assists. If we expand the list out to the Next 14 leagues, then only four players have more. Chelsea's Estêvão registered 23 goal contributions with Palmeiras in Brazil's top flight -- a much tougher league than MLS. Normally, I'd remove penalties from the equation, but the fact that Estevao was chosen to take three penalties as a 16-year-old feels like useful information.

Then there's Adu with 22, Romelu Lukaku with 19 for Anderlecht, and Endrick's 15 with Palmeiras before he moved to Real Madrid.

The smart money is on Sullivan moving up the list over the next month as MLS wraps up its regular season. In his eight games since the World Cup, he has scored six goals and added four assists.

132 passes into the attacking third
Sullivan is the rare attacking prospect whose attacking production actually underrates his track record.

Of course, the production at this point in his career is fantastic -- bested only by a collection of some of the best attacking prospects of the past 30 years. But that production is backed up by a sustainable drumbeat of quality shots and chances created, plus a bedrock of excellent ball progression and off-ball movement.

To dig into some more advanced numbers, we need to move beyond FBref's historical database. Stats Perform doesn't have numbers that extend to the 1990s, but we're able to look at the Big Five in Europe, MLS, Liga MX, the Dutch Eredivisie, the English second division, a number of cup competitions in Europe and South America, plus the first divisions in Portugal, Brazil, Argentina and Colombia. The data dates to at least the mid-2010s.

Among all of the players who fall within there, Sullivan ranks third and second, respectively, in the two most important and predictive attacking metrics: expected goals and expected assists. The other players I've highlighted in the below chart, which only looks at minutes played at age 16 or earlier, mostly played in more difficult leagues, but across the modern era of the sport almost no one has done what Sullivan is currently doing, still eight years away from the start of his prime:

He's also not just standing up near the goal and waiting for things to happen. Among this same cohort, Sullivan leads all players in passes played into the attacking third, with 132. The only other players with more than 100 are Jude Bellingham (104) and Gilberto Mora (109), both of whom are midfielders, not attackers.

That's clear when we look at passes played into the penalty area. Both Mora and Bellingham landed right around 100; Sullivan is all the way up at 202. Only Yamal, at 254, played more.

Scoring goals, creating chances, moving the ball into the attacking third, moving the ball into the box -- that's all there. The only thing missing is an ability to find space off of the ball, and it's only missing because I haven't mentioned it yet.

Sullivan has taken 142 touches inside the box. Among this cohort, Yamal, again, is the only player with more.

78 rating
The best players in modern soccer are the wide attackers who score goals, create chances, move the ball into attacking positions and find space inside the box. The best attacking prospects -- players in their late teens and early 20s -- tend to be able to score and create goals at a young age, but that's it. They usually can't aid in buildup play -- outside of slowing things down with a succession of head-down dribbles that sometimes move the ball upfield but often kill attacks by allowing the defense to recover. And they rarely have an advanced enough understanding of space and ball movement to be patient and savvy enough to receive passes in dangerous positions.

This all-conquering winger is a new prototype of player -- so new that the two best examples, Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, are still playing. And so we haven't seen many young players develop with this idea in mind. That is, until Yamal -- and yes, now Sullivan.

The just-turned-17-year-old doesn't just have good-for-a-16-year-old numbers in his first real professional season. No, he genuinely has been one of the best players in MLS.

The player-rating model from the stats app Futi looks at how much every touch increases or decreases his team's chances of scoring and conceding a goal. Then it adjusts for the player's role and how well his team plays when he's on and off the field. And finally, they convert it all into an easy-to-understand 0-to-100 scale.

Among players with at least 1,500 minutes played this season, Sullivan currently ranks in the top 10 for the Futi model. The average age of the players ahead of him is nearly twice his: 31. And that's all for the full season; if we looked only at the post-World-Cup stretch, he probably would be even higher:

There are still plenty of questions.

Will he grow? What happens when he has moved beyond Philadelphia's relatively chaotic system? How might he handle moving and living in Europe? Those questions -- and more -- would hold true for any 16-year-old soccer player.

But while it probably won't happen because it's an unlikely outcome for everyone who has ever lived, Sullivan's early-career excellence means that he is more likely to become a superstar than any American who has come before him.

Just consider this. Futi also rates each individual area of a player's in-possession performance: shooting, creating, receiving, dribbling and linking (or buildup play). There are two players in the league who rate above a 60 in all five.

The two: Cavan Sullivan and Lionel Messi.

stories.headline: White Sox strike first in AL wild card, beating Astros 6-3 in Game 1
stories.summary: — Colson Montgomery hit a solo homer and Sam Antonacci drove in two runs to lead the Chicago White Sox over the Houston Astros 6-3 in Game 1 of an AL Wild Card Series on Tuesday.
stories.body:
HOUSTON -- — Colson Montgomery hit a solo homer and Sam Antonacci drove in two runs to lead the Chicago White Sox over the Houston Astros 6-3 in Game 1 of an AL Wild Card Series on Tuesday.


The White Sox, in the postseason for the first time since 2021, made a remarkable turnaround this year to become the only team in major league history to follow consecutive 100-loss seasons with a playoff berth. They had lost 100 games three straight seasons, including 121 defeats in 2024, setting the record for most losses since 1899.


The White Sox got a letter of support from Pope Leo XIV, a Chicago native, prior to the game and got to work immediately to show off for the pontiff.


They led 3-0 after two innings and held on for their first playoff win since Oct. 10, 2021 in the ALDS against Houston.


The AL West-winning Astros eked into the playoffs with an 81-81 record to become the first team to reach the postseason without a winning record. Houston lost its eighth straight home playoff game in its ninth trip to the postseason in the last 10 years.


Game 2 in the best-of-three series is Wednesday in Houston.


Houston had runners on first and third with two outs in the eighth after singles by Jeremy Peña and MVP-favorite Yordan Alvarez when Jose Altuve reached and Peña scored on an error by third baseman Miguel Vargas to cut the lead to 6-3.


The Astros' tough day came in front of a surprisingly thin crowd. The announced attendance was 34,011 in a park with a capacity of 40,963. The home fans peppered the team with some boos when it fell behind early.


Both teams went with a bullpen game and combined to use 13 pitchers. Chicago opened with rookie left-hander Hagen Smith, and he allowed two hits in three scoreless innings.


Houston’s rookie opener AJ Blubaugh gave up two walks, and an error by Christian Walker left runners on first and third with one out in the first. The White Sox took an early lead on a sacrifice fly by Murakami.


Bryan King plunked Montgomery to load the bases with no outs in the second before Antonacci’s single pushed the lead to 3-0.


Montgomery, who manager Will Venable dropped to ninth in the order Tuesday, opened the fourth with a 432-foot homer to straightaway center field to make it 4-0. He hit 31 home runs in the regular season but also set the single-season record with 227 strikeouts.


Chicago made it 5-0 on a bases-loaded RBI single by Chase Meidroth with one out in the fifth.


Pinch-hitter Nelson Velázquez hit a two-run homer to cut the lead to 5-2 with two outs in the fifth.


The White Sox tacked on another run on a wild pitch by Bennett Sousa in the seventh.


Up next
Houston RHP Hunter Brown (6-4, 3.19 ERA) will start Game 2. The White Sox haven’t named a starter.

stories.headline: Which Premier League players got injured in the international break?
stories.summary: All the latest news and updates on Premier League stars injuries during the first international break of the 2026-2027 club season
stories.body:
Premier League teams will be watching and hoping their star players remain healthy throughout the international break.

However, some have already sustained injuries while playing for their countries. Premier League matches resume on Oct. 10.

ESPN will be tracking the latest injuries and updates for your club's players:

Kai Havertz (Arsenal)

Arsenal's Kai Havertz was forced off in the 30th minute of the game between Netherlands and Germany on September 24th with what was described as a muscle injury.

"Both are currently undergoing an MRI," Jurgen Klopp said on RTL about Havertz and Jamal Musiala. "I hope we get the diagnosis [on Thursday] evening. But of course, this isn't great. I hope it's nothing serious. The lads are probably out for us. But hopefully, they'll be back in action relatively quickly."

On September 25 the German Football Association confirmed the attacker would be leaving Klopp's camp and return to Arsenal after suffering what they describe as a 'muscle strain.'

Brian Brobbey (Sunderland)

The powerful Sunderland attacker was also injured in the same game after picking up what looked like a hamstring injury while running for the ball. He immediately went down and signalled to the sideline.

He left the field of his own accord but did have a heavy limp as he walked down the tunnel.

Netherlands boss Xavi Hernandez said after the game: "Brian is indeed injured."

Brobbey was replaced by Joshua Zirkzee in the Dutch squad.

Zion Suzuki (Aston Villa)

The goalkeeper linked up with the Japan squad but according to reports missed the main group training session on September 22nd, according to local reports. Instead he was put on an individual session for a rib injury.

Suzuki was subsequently left out of Japan's matchday squad entirely for Thursday's 3-1 victory over Uruguay.

Dan Ballard (Sunderland)

The Sunderland defender suffered a reported hamstring injury during Northern Ireland's 1-0 victory over Georgia in the UEFA Nations League.

With the score still 0-0 as the match moved into stoppage time, Ballard chased back as Georgia counter-attacked and pulled up clutching the back of his thigh, unable to finish the match in Tbilisi.

Speaking immediately after Friday's match, manager Michael O'Neill said it was too soon to know the extent of his latest injury but will definitely miss the next three Northern Ireland games.

"We'll scan him tomorrow (Saturday), but he's certainly not going to be available for the next three games."

Alexander Isak (Liverpool)

Alexander Isak is returning to Liverpool after sustaining a "minor injury" on international duty.

The striker scored and played the full 90 minutes in Sweden's 2-1 victory over Romania in the Nations League on Friday.

But Isak, who has made a strong start to the season for Liverpool, will not feature in matches against Poland, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Romania over the remainder of the extended international break.

Bruno Fernandes (Manchester United)

The Manchester United midfielder was left out of Portugal's squad for Sunday's game against Norway.

"He played with an injury he brought from Manchester United," Portugal boss Jorge Jesus said. "He really wanted to play against Wales."

Patrick Dorgu (Manchester United)

The news for Manchester United fans who saw Fernandes absent worsened on Sunday when Dorgu was injured.

The left wing-back limped out of Denmark's match against Wales after 30 minutes.

Denmark head coach Brian Riemer told broadcaster TV2 after the game: "He has an injury and has to go home."

Cody Gakpo (Liverpool)

Liverpool forward Gakpo lasted only 17 minutes of the Netherlands' match against Serbia on Sunday. It means Liverpool are sweating over the fitness of Isak and Gakpo.

He looked in pain as he held the lower part of his right leg.

"It's his ankle, that's all I know," Netherlands boss Xavi Hernández said. "Tomorrow we will know, but hopefully it's not too important."

Noussair Mazraoui (Manchester United)

The United full-back was forced out of Morocco's Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Lesotho after 69 minutes. He was holding his back while on the floor after a challenge.

Nico O'Reilly (Manchester City)

O'Reilly missed England's win against Czechia on Tuesday night after also missing training on Monday. Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha was called into the matchday squad.

International breaks this season

1. Sept. 21-Oct. 6 (between Premier League gameweeks 5 and 6)

2. Nov. 9-Nov. 17 (between Premier League gameweeks 10 and 11)

3. March 22-March 30 (between Premier League gameweeks 30 and 31)

stories.headline: PSG chief Al-Khelaifi has 'zero interest' in FIFA presidency
stories.summary: European soccer's search for a candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino in the FIFA presidential election will not land on clubs' leader Nasser Al-Khelaifi.
stories.body:
GENEVA -- European soccer's search for a candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino in the FIFA presidential election will not land on clubs' leader Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Paris Saint-Germain boss insisted Tuesday.

Al-Khelaifi also is chairman of the influential European Football Clubs group and so sits on the executive committee of UEFA, which is leading efforts to oust Infantino after his failed plan to sell stakes in future World Cup profits to private investors.

- Will anyone stop Infantino? FIFA president is confident U20 World Cup cameo says otherwise

- FIFA agrees in principle to federation payments from WC windfall

- FIFA accuses UEFA of 'misinformation campaign' over World Cup proposal

As a minister in the government of 2022 World Cup host Qatar -- which has so far supported Infantino -- Al-Khelaifi also could have broad appeal to FIFA voters in Asia, yet he moved to quash speculation he might try to lead soccer's governing body.

"I have zero interest in FIFA, zero agenda [or] ambition to be there," Al-Khelaifi said at a news conference after an EFC annual meeting in the Danish capital Copenhagen.

"I don't think I'm the right guy for this position and I don't want to go actually, I'm enjoying what I'm doing," the president of Champions League title holders PSG said. "I think FIFA's not for me. Thank you."

The annual meeting of the 900-member club was held amid a volatile time for soccer politics and Infantino's future.

It is two months after Infantino's multi-billion dollar FIFA subsidiary plan was revealed, then defeated within days, and seven weeks before the deadline for candidates to challenge him.

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin is leading the campaign to end Infantino's presidency either before or at the March 18 election in Morocco, and he spoke to club leaders Tuesday.

"Football has no need for emperors," Ceferin said in a near 10-minute speech that did not name Infantino, whose biggest plans since his first election in 2016 have typically been seen as threats by his former employers at UEFA.

Ceferin's references, including creating an award for a politician, were clearly aimed at Infantino and his close working relations with U.S. President Donald Trump.

"It's time to say enough," said Ceferin, a FIFA vice president who has ruled himself out of being a candidate. "Rules bent when inconvenient. Those meant to have a say simply cut out. And football's future treated as just another bargaining chip."

Ceferin, like Infantino, was elected in 2016 -- in the fallout of FIFA's previous biggest crisis, provoked by U.S. and Swiss federal investigations -- and also can seek a fourth and final term in office next year.

"Football needs great leaders like you," Al-Khelaifi said of Ceferin in his own speech, adding "we ask you to stand for president again next year."

Ceferin, who said in 2024 he would leave office in 2027, is likely to be unopposed in the UEFA vote by 55 member federations scheduled in April in Astana, Kazakhstan.
